summary: This standards-track RFC describes the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm, which translates between IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers, including ICMP headers. It obsoletes RFC 6145.

plainLanguage.summary: A translator that rewrites the envelope of a message from one addressing style to another without remembering anything.

questions: how does ipv4 to ipv6 translation work
what is the difference between stateless and stateful translation
how are icmp messages translated between ipv4 and ipv6
subtitle: How a router rewrites IPv4 packets into IPv6 packets, and back again, without keeping any per-connection state.

tldr.problem: IPv4-only and IPv6-only systems cannot talk to each other directly, because the packet headers, ICMP messages and minimum packet sizes differ.
tldr.mechanism: A translator (XLAT) removes the IPv4 header and replaces it with an IPv6 header, or the reverse, field by field. It also translates ICMP messages and fixes transport checksums, using only its configuration and the packet itself.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7915 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 6145. It adds notes on IPv6 extension headers and drops the generation of IPv6 atomic fragments.

today: RFC 7915 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 6145 and is the current definition of the stateless IP/ICMP translation algorithm in this record.

sections.title: What the Translator Does
sections.content:
RFC 7915 describes the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm (SIIT). It translates between IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers, including ICMP headers. It obsoletes RFC 6145, and readers are expected to know the framework in RFC 6144.

The model is simple: two or more network domains are joined by one or more IP/ICMP translators, called XLATs. When a packet crosses from one domain to the other, the XLAT removes the old IP header and puts a new one in its place. The data portion of the packet is left unchanged.

There are limits. The translator does not translate any IPv4 options, and it does not translate IPv6 extension headers except the Fragment Header. Fragmented ICMP and ICMPv6 packets are not translated. IPv4 multicast addresses cannot be mapped to IPv6 multicast addresses with the unicast mapping rule.
sections.plainLanguage: A translator sits between an old-style network and a new-style network. It swaps the outside label on each packet and leaves what is inside alone.

sections.title: Stateless Versus Stateful Translation
sections.content:
A translator can work in two modes. In stateless mode it converts addresses solely from its own configuration and from information in the packet being translated. It keeps no dynamic session or binding state, so packets of one flow do not have to pass through the same translator.

In stateful mode the translator keeps a dynamic table of bindings between IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, and likely Layer-4 identifiers. The translation of one packet then depends on how earlier packets in the flow were translated, so all packets of a flow generally have to traverse the same translator.

This RFC is about the algorithm for the headers. It does not define any address mapping algorithm itself; it refers to them in its Section 6. Stateful behavior is left to documents such as RFC 6146.
sections.plainLanguage: A stateless translator is a clerk who works only from the rule book and the letter in hand. A stateful clerk also keeps a notebook of every conversation, so the same clerk has to handle the whole conversation.

sections.title: Translating IPv4 Headers into IPv6
sections.content:
For an IPv4 packet heading into the IPv6 domain, the translator replaces the IPv4 header with an IPv6 header. By default the Traffic Class is copied from the IPv4 TOS octet, the Flow Label is 0, and the Payload Length is the IPv4 total length minus the IPv4 header and any options. The Next Header value is copied from the Protocol field, except that ICMPv4 (1) becomes ICMPv6 (58). The hop limit is derived from the TTL, and the translator, being a router, MUST check for zero and send the matching error.

IPv4 options are ignored and the packet is translated normally. The exception is an unexpired source route option: then the packet MUST be discarded and an ICMPv4 Destination Unreachable, Source Route Failed (Type 3, Code 5) message SHOULD be returned. Packets with an illegal source address such as 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1 SHOULD be silently discarded.

Size differences need care. IPv6 routers never fragment, and the minimum IPv6 MTU is 1280 bytes. If the DF bit is not set and the result would exceed a configurable lowest-ipv6-mtu (default 1280), the packet SHOULD be fragmented first so the IPv4 payload is at most 1232 bytes: 1280 minus 40 for the IPv6 header and 8 for the Fragment Header. The translator MUST let an administrator raise that threshold above 1280. When fragments exist, the IPv6 Fragment Header carries the offset and More Fragments bit from IPv4, and the low-order 16 bits of the identification, with the high-order 16 bits set to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator throws away the old address label and writes a new one, copying over things like how urgent the packet is. If the packet is too big for the new network, it is cut into smaller pieces first.

sections.title: Translating IPv6 Headers into IPv4
sections.content:
Going the other way, the translator replaces the IPv6 header with an IPv4 header. The Version is 4 and the Internet Header Length is 5, since no IPv4 options are produced. The TOS octet is copied from the Traffic Class by default, the Identification comes from a generator at the translator, and the Header Checksum is computed once the header exists. Next Header 58 (ICMPv6) becomes Protocol 1 (ICMPv4).

The Don't Fragment bit is set to zero if the translated IPv4 packet is 1260 bytes or smaller, and to one otherwise. That keeps path MTU discovery working end to end for paths whose MTU is not below the IPv6 minimum of 1280, which corresponds to 1260 in the IPv4 domain.

Extension headers are mostly skipped. Hop-by-Hop (0), Routing (43) and Destination Options (60) headers with a Routing Segments Left of zero are ignored and the packet is translated. A Routing header with a non-zero Segments Left means the packet MUST NOT be translated, and an ICMPv6 Parameter Problem (Type 4, Code 0) SHOULD be returned. If a Fragment Header is present, its offset and M flag are copied, DF is cleared, and a packet whose Fragment Header is followed by another extension header (except ESP) SHOULD be dropped and logged.
sections.plainLanguage: Going back to the old network, the translator writes the old-style label again. It also decides whether the packet is small enough that it does not need to be protected from being chopped up on the way.

sections.title: Translating ICMP Messages
sections.content:
ICMP needs its own rules because ICMPv6, unlike ICMPv4, has a pseudo-header in its checksum. Every translated ICMP message has its checksum recalculated, its Type translated, and, for errors, the embedded packet in error translated like any other packet. This stops at the first embedded header: if more headers are nested, the packet is dropped.

Echo and Echo Reply map between types 8 and 0 and types 128 and 129. Destination Unreachable (3) becomes type 1 with the Code mapped, Time Exceeded (11) becomes 3 and Parameter Problem (12) becomes 4. A Fragmentation Needed message (Type 3, Code 4) becomes ICMPv6 Packet Too Big (Type 2), and its MTU is adjusted for the header size difference but MUST NOT go below 1280. Messages that have no useful counterpart, such as Timestamp, Information, Address Mask, Router Advertisement and Solicitation, Redirect and Source Quench, are silently dropped, as are unknown types and single-hop IGMP messages.

When the translator discards a packet, it SHOULD send an error unless the dropped packet was itself an ICMP error. On the IPv6 side the error MUST be Type 1, Code 1 unless the RFC says otherwise. Administrators SHOULD be able to configure whether these errors are sent, rate-limited or not sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages like 'that address does not exist' have to be reworded so the other side understands them. Messages that only make sense on one kind of network are simply thrown away.

sections.title: Address Mapping and Transport Checksums
sections.content:
The translator needs an address mapping algorithm to turn IPv4 addresses into IPv6 ones and back. It MUST support the stateless algorithm of RFC 6052, which is the default. It SHOULD support the explicit address mapping algorithm of RFC 7757, and it SHOULD support RFC 6791 for handling ICMP and ICMPv6 packets. The RFC also notes that an implementation may do stateful NAT64 (RFC 6146) or stateless MAP-T (RFC 7599) functions.

If the mapping is not checksum neutral, the checksums in transport headers that cover the IP pseudo-header must be recalculated. Translators MUST do this for TCP and ICMP, and for UDP with a non-zero checksum. For IPv4 UDP packets with a zero checksum, the translator SHOULD offer a choice: drop the packet and log an event, or compute an IPv6 checksum and forward it. A stateless translator cannot compute the checksum of fragmented UDP packets, so it SHOULD drop a first fragment whose checksum is zero. Other transports such as DCCP are optional, but translators MUST still forward all transport protocols.

If the translator also forwards normally and a more specific route exists without translation, it MUST forward the packet untranslated.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator needs a rule for turning one kind of address into the other. If the rule changes numbers that are used in a packet's error check, the check has to be redone so the packet is not rejected.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Packet Too Big
sections.content:
RFC 7915 says stateless translators introduce no new security issues beyond those already present in IPv4, IPv6 and the routing protocols that deliver packets to the translator. Deriving an IPv4 address from an IPv6 address can still produce problem cases such as broadcast, loopback or non-IPv4-translatable addresses, which RFC 6052 addresses.

IPsec interacts poorly with translation. The IPsec Authentication Header cannot be used for NAT44 or NAT64. Tunnel mode ESP can be translated, while transport mode ESP fails on IPv6-to-IPv4 translation unless checksum-neutral addresses are used. In both cases, ESP endpoints will normally detect the translator and wrap ESP in UDP.

Section 7 adds an operational warning: studies indicate that networks often drop ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages. Those drops cause path MTU discovery black holes, which can only be overcome with Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: Translating does not open new holes by itself. But some secret-keeping envelopes do not survive being re-addressed, and if the 'your packet is too big' notes get lost, the sender never learns to send smaller ones.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
Appendix A walks through a stateless translation using documentation address blocks. The XLAT uses the Network-Specific Prefix 2001:db8:100::/40 from RFC 6052. The IPv6 host H6 has the IPv4-translatable address 2001:db8:1c0:2:21::, which maps from 192.0.2.33. The IPv4 host H4 has the address 198.51.100.2.

H6 forms the destination 2001:db8:1c6:3364:2:: from 198.51.100.2 and sends a packet. Routing delivers it to the XLAT, which translates the header and sends it out its IPv4 interface with source 192.0.2.33 and destination 198.51.100.2. The addresses are read directly out of the IPv6 addresses, with no table lookup. H4's reply is translated back the same way. The same works when H4 starts the conversation.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows two friends on different kinds of networks swapping messages through the translator. Each address can be worked out from the other by a fixed rule, so the translator never needs to look anything up.
